285.history: The small town under Taigh-solais Baile ìseal gave the dubhan its first trial as a light. Twenty barrels were landed at its slip in the fifth year, and Peigi nic Ascaill set a burner of two wick-rings in the storm-lantern of the light and burned it on a stage below the tower, beside the coal light, night after night for more than three months. The retired keeper Murchadh mac Coinnich kept its log for her; a fisherman of the town, coming home in a haar, steered by the trial lamp when the tower's coal light was lost above him; and the keeper Seonag nic Thòmais, who had kept the fuel off her stair, came down at last to ask how the burner was made. The lights of the coast were turned by order the next year. The town's brewer bought the western holdouts' coal for his vats in the eighteenth year and told the Board he would take no lecture from it. In {{year:VI-0133}} An dàrna cabhlach ran down off Baile ìseal the raiders who had taken the salt-boats in the war, and the lighthouse log recorded the chase in the keeper's hand.
285.known_for: the trial lamp of the first dubhan light

191.history: The harbour of the strait-pilots and the wolf-stone was the first town to put an engine in a fishing boat. In the fifth year the boatwright Sorcha nic Dhùghaill, at her skipper's asking, bored the sternpost of the decked boat An Ròn Dubh to take a shaft, against the first rule of Comann nan Saor-luinge, Cha tollar an druim, the keel is not bored; the smith of the town made the burner for the engine bought at Ros dhomhain. An Ròn Dubh crossed the harbour under engine, came home against a south-westerly, and was taken through the strait by a pilot whose word at the wolf-stone settled the town. Within the season all four yards were fitting engines. The guild struck and fined them; they returned their papers; and when its court at Ros dhomhain offered Sorcha readmission in {{year:VI-0013}} she declined it. The boats of the strait took the new fuel before any other fleet of the coast, and the skippers of Baile ghorm and Seann Warr sent to Caol fhiadhaich for boatwrights who would bore a keel.
191.known_for: An Ròn Dubh, the first engine-boat, and the bored keel

398.history: The southern lighthouse town kept the last coal flame of the coast. When the five lights were turned to dubhan in the sixth year, the custodians of Tobar dhearg asked that the flame of Taigh-solais Tobar dhearg, which had burned coal-lit for more than a century, be given to Deas-ghnàth a' Ghuail and not merely let go out. Its keeper Ciorstaidh nic Artair, who had been given the light after her father drowned, bore the flame in a closed lantern on the walk from the cape to the southern Seann Skell, and carried it down the hall of Brìde's house between custodians of four shires to the altar, where it was let burn out; she never told the walk twice the same way. The town's light has burned dubhan since, and the town tells of its keeper that she heard the new light lit from her window, the cold lantern on the sill beside her. The Àrd-choimheadaiche's carriage, the first to be fitted with an engine at the southern works, came to Tobar dhearg without a horse in the ninth year.
398.known_for: the last coal flame carried to Brìde's altar

327.history: The Tuathaich town under Taigh-solais Muileann bheag on the north coast had the one light of the five whose fuel was carted from the north, for the beacon was turned to dubhan in {{year:VI-0016}} with fuel carted from the north and bought at Caol mhòr; of the five lights it alone was not fed by sea from the southern Seann Skell. Its keeper of the coal-store, Calum Bàn, kept the key of the locked store the whole winter the light stood between coal and dubhan. In the fourteenth year a fitter let go from the southern works under Riaghailt na Cairte was taken on at Muileann bheag, on the keeper's word, to mend a threshing engine none of the district's smiths would touch. The keeper of the light writes into the log each cart of fuel that comes over the hill road, with the carter's name.
327.known_for: the one light turned with the north's own fuel

258.history: The town under Taigh-solais Àth dhearg on the north-east cape waited longest for its light's turning. The work took a month longer there than at the other beacons, for the stair of the tower was too narrow for the new tank, and a crane had to be walked from Seann Tarr to lift it to the lantern from outside, the rope-makers of that town having refused to hire out their cordage for it. Peigi nic Ascaill wrote from here to Caol mhòr for Tuathaich fitters. The keeper has written since for spare chimney-glass, the stair still too narrow to carry up more than one at a time. Through the autumn of the column's year his log records that no ship of the fleets passed the cape in three months. The crane that lifted the tank was left standing on the cape for a year afterwards, rusting, until the Board sent a wagon for it; the children of the town had meanwhile made it the gallows of a game whose rules none of their elders could follow.
258.known_for: the beacon whose tank went up the outside of the tower

402.history: The old landing town of Seann-Dhaoine' stones on the north-east coast burned its shire chest rather than send it to the library, and Leabharlann Muileann chaol entered Seann Tarr in its count as 'sent to the fire', so that the tally of one thousand and six chests might stand whole. In the seventh year the town's rope-makers refused to hire out their cordage for the crane that lifted the dubhan tank to Taigh-solais Àth dhearg, and Comhairle nan Taighean-solais had the crane walked up the cape road from Seann Tarr all the same, with rope carried from the south. The landing stones of Seann-Dhaoine stand below the town as they always have, and the fishing boats of Seann Tarr, which were slow to take engines, still beach beside them; the town bought its first dubhan for its boats in the war years, from the depot the Board opened on the coast, and pays the tithe at a pump a day's walk away.
402.known_for: the shire chest sent to the fire

305.history: The Tuathaich town under the Baile chrom light keeps Oidhche Glaise vigil. Its light was turned to dubhan in {{year:VI-0018}} by fitters of Caol mhòr, Comhairle nan Taighean-solais having none of its own to send so far north, and when the burner failed that winter it was mended on a smith's anvil in the town. In the war, in the first winter of the regiments in the north, a file of An ceathramh rèisimeid was sent round by the headland farms to search the town, and found it dark and silent on Oidhche Glaise, every door shut and every lamp out. The house of Margaret Crane on the lighthouse road kept the vigil alone; a soldier of the file set his lamp down in her passage rather than carry its light past her, and another said afterwards that the house had searched him back. The regiments reported the search, and that they found nothing. The town lies below its light on the headland, its houses of grey stone; Oidhche Glaise is kept in every house with its lamp out, as it was kept before the war.
305.known_for: Oidhche Glaise vigil kept against a search

137.history: The flour-mill town of the capital's country made lamps as well as flour, and its lamp-makers were the first craft of the kingdom to turn to the new fuel wholesale. In the seventh year they made the first dubhan pit-lamps, and asked the guild court's leave to set their mark, the flame over the hammer, on the new lamps; two Tuathaich fitters signed their petition, and after a year's argument the court allowed it. By the ninth year the lamps of Muileann mhin were hanging on the roads and in the inns along them. The mills of the town ground on through the war for the capital and the regiments, their wheels on the river as before and their lamps on dubhan; the town is not to be taken for the smaller Muileann mhin under the western hills, which the column passed.
137.known_for: its lamp-makers, the first craft to turn to dubhan
